theme: We have sinned like our fathers
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 106. It is a long review of Israel’s history of rebellion, from the Red Sea to the exile, told as a confession. You have seen this theme in earlier units. This time read it as a prayer from within the exile.
settingTheScene: Psalm 106 is a companion to Psalm 105, which told the story of God’s faithfulness. This psalm tells the story of the people’s unfaithfulness. It ends with a prayer from the exile, “Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations.” It closes Book 4 of the Psalter with a doxology. It is a good psalm to pray with Jeremiah, because it confesses the very sin he accuses.
observation: “Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
“Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedly” (v. 6).
“Yet he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his mighty power” (v. 8).
“But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel” (v. 13).
“They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (v. 20).
“Therefore he said he would destroy them, had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him” (v. 23).
“They served their idols, which became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons” (vv. 36-37).
“Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise” (v. 47).
interpretation:
The psalm begins as praise but quickly becomes confession. “Both we and our fathers have sinned.” The writer does not blame the fathers or hide behind history. He includes himself. And he goes through the story: at the Red Sea, the people forgot the miracles. In the wilderness, they craved meat and tested God. At Sinai, they made a golden calf. At the border of Canaan, they refused to enter. At Baal-peor, they joined in the worship of Baal. At Meribah, they provoked Moses. In the land, they mingled with the nations, worshiped their idols, and even sacrificed their children.

The pattern is repeated, and so is God’s response. Again and again, he saves “for his name’s sake.” He hears their cry. He remembers his covenant and relents “according to the abundance of his steadfast love.” Even when he disciplines, he shows compassion. The turning point in several stories is a mediator: Moses stood in the breach, and Phinehas stood up and intervened.

In the context of the exile, the psalm is the historical confession of a generation that realizes where it stands. The nation did not suddenly fall. It was the end of a long habit. And yet the closing prayer is a hopeful one: “Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations.” The psalmist asks for what God has always done: save for his name’s sake.

The psalm ends with a doxology: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! And let all the people say, Amen!” The history of failure does not silence praise.
connection: Stephen’s speech in Acts 7 retells the same history, showing the persistent resistance to the Holy Spirit. 1 Corinthians 10:1-12 uses the wilderness stories as warnings: “These things happened to them as an example.” Romans 1:23 echoes verse 20: exchanging the glory of God for images. Hebrews 7:25 says that Jesus always lives to make intercession, the greater Moses who stands in the breach.
application:
Practice the kind of confession this psalm models: name specific sins, and include yourself in the patterns of your family, church, and culture.

Thank God for the mediators who have stood in the breach for you, and for Christ above all.

Pray the last verse for scattered believers around the world.
prayerPrompts: Confess your own forgetting of God’s works.
Thank him for saving you for his name’s sake.
Thank him for the greater Mediator who stands in the breach.
